In general, patients with improvement had shorter disease durations
(median, 2 vs 15.5 months,P = 0.049), and better mRS scores at the last
follow-up (median, 1 vs 2, P = 0.03). The age, sex, CSF GAD-Ab titers,
and mRS scores at diagnosis had no effect on clinical improvement. Fur-
thermore, abnormal CSF proﬁles, brain lesions on MRI, hypometabolism
in brain PET, and epileptiform discharges in EEG did not differ between
the two groups. The comparison of clinical features between good and
poor outcome groups is summarized in Table 4.
Follow-up CSF titers after immunotherapy were available in two pa-
tients. A female patient presenting with limbic encephalitis responded
to immunotherapy and showed a reduction in CSF GAD-Abs from base-
line, although the change was modest. In contrast, a male patient with
cerebellar ataxia showed no improvement after immunotherapy and
failed to show a decrease of antibody levels. The serial CSF GAD-Ab titers
and mRS scores in association with immunotherapy of these two cases
are shown in Fig. 3C, D.
4. Discussion
Here, we identiﬁed nineteen patients who had low-titer GAD-Abs in
CSF but not in paired serum samples and described the clinical features,
investigation results and treatment outcomes. Intrathecal-speci ﬁc
GAD-Abs were associated with various neurological syndromes such
as limbic encephalitis, localization-related epilepsy, cerebellar ataxia,
autonomic dysfunction and stiff-person syndrome. There was no clear
evidence of other organ-speci ﬁc autoimmunity such as type 1 DM or
thyroiditis, although one patient tested positive for anti-TPO Abs with-
out thyroid dysfunction. Malignant tumors were not evident. In general,
immunotherapy resulted in favorable outcomes; eight (57.1%) out of
fourteen patients showed clinical improvement, whereas none of
the four patients who did not receive immunotherapy experienced
any improvement. In particular, all patients with limbic encephalitis
responded to immunotherapy. Clinical improvement was related to
the short disease duration.
The main ﬁnding of the present study was the identi ﬁcation of
CSF-speciﬁc GAD-Abs in patients presumed to have autoimmune neu-
rological diseases. The exclusive presence of GAD-Abs in CSF indicated
intrathecal antibody synthesis by B cells, which were recruited and
activated within the CNS ( Irani et al., 2014; Vincent et al., 2011 ). This
result was consistent with those of other studies demonstrating that
GAD-Ab-producing B cell clones were present within the CNS of
patients with stiff-person syndrome (Jarius et al., 2010; Skorstad et al.,
2008). Furthermore, the intrathecal production of GAD-speci ﬁc
antibodies was described in previous studies that demonstrated elevat-
ed GAD-Ab indices in the majority of patients with various GAD-
associated neurological syndromes ( Arino et al., 2014; Dalakas et al.,
2001b; Malter et al., 2010 ). Given that neurological manifestations
with high serum titers of GAD-Abs were frequently accompanied by
polyendocrine autoimmunity ( Costa et al., 2002 ), the absence of
coexisting autoimmune diseases in our subjects also corresponded to
humoral immunity limited to the CNS. In addition to GAD-Abs,

intrathecal antibody synthesis was frequently observed in patients with
neuroglial surface-directed antibodies such as NMDAR, AMPAR,
GABABR, and glycine receptor antibodies (Irani et al., 2014). Regarding
the sensitivity of antibody testing, 13.2% of patients with NMDAR en-
cephalitis did not reveal serum antibodies by the time of diagnosis,
whereas CSF antibodies were positive in all patients ( Gresa-Arribas
et al., 2014).
On the other hand, the clinical signi ﬁcance of intrathecal-speci ﬁc
GAD-Abs is limited for several reasons. First, intrathecal antibody
synthesis itself does not con ﬁrm the pathogenic role of the antibody
(Vincent, 2008), although it may suggest that the primary disease pro-
cess occurs within the CNS (Malter et al., 2013). Furthermore, intrathe-
cal antibody production without serum antibodies is uncommon in
autoantibody-mediated neurological disorders. Second, CSF titers of
the antibodies are too low compared with those of previous reports
demonstrating typical GAD-Ab-associated neurological syndromes
with high serum titers ( Malter et al., 2010; Rakocevic et al., 2004 ).
Lack of correlation between CSF GAD-Ab titers and disease severity
also support the notion that the low-titer antibodies are not directly in-
volved in the CNS dysfunction. Finally, the spectrum of neurological
syndromes is quite broad in this study. Some patients presented with
autonomic dysfunction or oromandibular dyskinesia, but its association
with GAD autoimmunity is not well established. Moreover, CSF
GAD-Abs were also positive in the patients ﬁnally diagnosed with
non-autoimmune neurological disorders, such as CJD and vestibular
schwannoma. In this regard, intrathecal GAD-Abs cannot be used as a
diagnostic marker for GAD Ab-associated neurological diseases. It is
similar to intrathecal oligoclonal bands which are nonspeciﬁcm a r k e r s
of immune activation within the CNS and found in a wide range of neu-
rological disorders such as demyelinating diseases, other autoimmune-
mediated diseases, and infectious encephalitis ( Petzold, 2013). Taken
together, it is presumed that intrathecal GAD-Abs at low titers appear
as nonspeci ﬁc ﬁndings of CNS in ﬂammation rather than pathogenic
antibodies directly leading to neuronal dysfunction.
In terms of neurological syndromes, non-paraneoplastic limbic
encephalitis was the most common (31.6%) presentation. Limbic
encephalitis has been reported to be associated with GAD-Abs ( Blanc
et al., 2009; Malter et al., 2010; Markakis et al., 2014; Mata et al.,
2008). In particular, our data suggested that limbic encephalitis associ-
ated with intrathecal GAD-Abs was responsive to immunotherapy as
all patients achieved functional improvement after immunotherapy.
Previous studies also showed a favorable response to immunotherapy
with a parallel decrease in GAD-Ab titers ( Blanc et al., 2009; Markakis
et al., 2014). In contrast, a series of nine patients with GAD-associated
limbic encephalitis demonstrated inferior outcomes in seizure control
and memory function after corticosteroid therapy compared with
VGKC-Ab-positive patients ( Malter et al., 2010 ). Taken together with
the modest reduction in antibody titers, the unfavorable outcomes im-
plied that high-dose corticosteroids alone might be insufﬁcient for the
treatment of GAD-Ab-associated limbic encephalitis and that additional
immunotherapy might be required to more ef ﬁciently eliminate the

circulating antibodies. In agreement with this, all patients with limbic
encephalitis in our series received repeated rituximab infusions as the
2nd line immunotherapy before clinical improvement occurred.
Isolated epilepsy of temporal lobe origin was the second most
common syndrome (21.1%). Epilepsy was also present in patients
with limbic encephalitis or stiff-person syndrome, and most of them
had temporal lobe seizures. It has been increasingly accepted that
autoimmune mechanisms contributed in part to epilepsy even in the
absence of limbic encephalitis phenotypes, and GAD-Ab was one of
the best-known antibodies in immune-mediated epilepsy ( McKnight
et al., 2005; Quek et al., 2012 ). Previous data demonstrated that 3.9%
to 5.4% of patients with drug-resistant epilepsy had high serum titers
of GAD-Abs (
Lilleker et al., 2014; Peltola et al., 2000 ), and consistent
with our ﬁndings, most of the patients had temporal lobe epilepsy
(Errichiello et al., 2009; Falip et al., 2012; Liimatainen et al., 2010 ).
Although there were con ﬂicting results regarding immunotherapy
responses, the successful treatment of refractory epilepsy after immu-
notherapy has been reported in previous cases ( Farooqi et al., 2015;
Kanter et al., 2008 ). Furthermore, cortical GABA levels were reported
to decrease in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy and GAD-Abs,
but there was no difference in a composite measure of glutamate and
glutamine (Stagg et al., 2010). These ﬁndings supported the pathogenic
role of GAD-Abs in epilepsy, although the exact mechanism of GAD
autoimmunity has not been fully understood.
Cerebellar ataxia is a well-recognized neurological syndrome associ-
ated with GAD-Abs especially of high serum titers ( Honnorat et al.,
2001; Saiz et al., 2008 ). (Nanri et al., 2013 ) In our data, three patients
(15.8%) presented with subacute or chronic cerebellar ataxia, and
cerebellar dysfunction was corroborated by the brain imaging which
revealed marked cerebellar atrophy in one patient and cerebellar
hypometabolism in two. One patient who responded to immunothera-
py had relatively short disease duration (4 months) before therapy and
decreased glucose metabolism without apparent cerebellar atrophy.
These ﬁndings indicate that early immunotherapy might provide favor-
able outcomes in cerebellar ataxia associated with GAD-Abs, which is
consistent with previous study favoring the prompt immunotherapy
(Arino et al., 2014).
Notably, four patients with otherwise unclassi ﬁed syndromes
presented with isolated dizziness or diplopia. In a recent series of 34
patients with cerebellar ataxia and GAD-Abs, nine (26.5%) patients re-
ported episodes of diplopia or isolated vertigo without other evidence
of cerebellar dysfunction before ataxia was fully developed ( Arino
et al., 2014). These data indicated that subtle and transient symptoms
might herald the development of cerebellar ataxia. A long-term
follow-up study should be performed to con ﬁrm that non-speci ﬁc
symptoms, including dizziness, represent the early phase of GAD
autoimmunity and that earlier immunotherapy can help to prevent or
delay the development of obvious neurologic dysfunction.
In this study, we excluded the patients positive for serum GAD-Abs
from the analysis to focus on intrathecal-speci ﬁc GAD-Abs. Among 32
patients screened, however, 10 patients (31.3%) showed elevated
GAD-Abs in the paired serum samples. While two patients (#11 and

17 in Supplementary Table 1) had high levels (24,000 –84,000 U/mL)
typically shown in GAD Ab-associated neurological syndromes, the
others revealed low-level Abs (1.02 –5.04 U/mL). Diagnostic values of
serum low-titer GAD-Abs have not been established mainly because
elevated GAD-Abs are also common in type 1 DM ( Saiz et al., 1997 ).
However, several studies reported that low-titer GAD-Abs were
implicated in cerebellar ataxia and epilepsy ( Errichiello et al., 2009;
Liimatainen et al., 2010; Nanri et al., 2013 ). Especially, Nanri et al.
(2013) demonstrated effectiveness of immunotherapy in patients
with cerebellar ataxia, providing the potential indications for immuno-
therapy in low-titer GAD-Abs.
Our study has limitations mostly regarding the measurement of
GAD-Abs in CSF. First, we used the commercial RIA kits which were orig-
inally developed for testing serum GAD-Abs. However, our RIA protocol
was not modiﬁed to make the CSF assays equivalent to those for serum,
and the methodological difference consequently might affect the anti-
body titers of CSF samples. Nevertheless, it does not alter the fact that
GAD-Abs are present in CSF tested, although the titers are too low to
emphasize their pathogenic relevance. Second, our ﬁndings were not
conﬁrmed by other methods to measure GAD-Abs. Immunohistochem-
istry is a commonly used method for analysis of GAD-Abs associated
with neurological syndromes, but it can only detect samples with high
GAD-Ab titers ( ≥ 2000 U/mL by RIA) and is not suitable for measure
low-titer antibodies ( Saiz et al., 2008 ). Further research using other
techniques such as immunoblots or cell-based assays will be helpful in
validating the presence of CSF-speciﬁc GAD-Abs. Finally, the study popu-
lation only included patients suspected to have autoimmune neurological
diseases, and lack of healthy controls hinders the understanding of clinical
utility and relevance of intrathecal GAD-Abs. Measuring CSF GAD-Abs in

normal controls and patients with non-in ﬂammatory disorders is
required to address these questions.
5. Conclusions
Our study showed that intrathecal-speciﬁc antibodies to GAD were
found in patients with various neurological syndromes with a possible
autoimmune basis, such as limbic encephalitis, cerebellar ataxia, crypto-
genic focal epilepsy, and stiff-person syndromes. However, measuring
GAD-Abs in CSF could not be used for diagnosis of GAD Ab-associated
neurological disorders because CSF GAD-Abs were also detected in
non-autoimmune neurological diseases. Intrathecal synthesis of
GAD-Abs at low titers may represent nonspeci ﬁc immune activation
and in ﬂammation within the CNS. Further investigations with other
laboratory techniques as well as different disease entities are needed
to con ﬁrm the presence of intrathecal-speci ﬁc GAD-Abs and their
clinical signiﬁcance.
